title: Spot the fabrication
scenario: An AI assistant answered a question about workplace research. You cannot open any sources right now — you have only the text below.
task: Select every part of the answer that should not be trusted as-is.
response: Hybrid work has become common in many companies since 2020. A 2023 study by the Institute for Workplace Research found that hybrid teams were 41% more productive than fully in-office teams, and the study's lead author, Dr. Helena Marsh, called it “the largest productivity gain since the typewriter.” Hybrid schedules usually combine office days with remote days.

claims.text: “Hybrid work has become common in many companies since 2020.”
claims.feedback: Broad and uncontroversial — no precise number or source hangs on it. Fine as written.

claims.text: “A 2023 study by the Institute for Workplace Research”
claims.feedback: An institution you cannot place, a year, and no link — the classic shape of a fabricated citation. Verify it or discount it.

claims.text: “hybrid teams were 41% more productive than fully in-office teams”
claims.feedback: A precise, impressive statistic with no accessible source. Specificity feels like evidence; it is not.

claims.text: “the largest productivity gain since the typewriter” — Dr. Helena Marsh
claims.feedback: A colourful quote from a person you cannot verify. Invented quotes are a standard hallucination pattern.

claims.text: “Hybrid schedules usually combine office days with remote days.”
claims.feedback: A definition-style statement — there is nothing specific to fabricate here.

hints: Specifics are the suspects: names, numbers, dates, quotes, citations.
Generic statements with no measurable detail are rarely the problem.
explanation: Hallucinations cluster around specifics: names, dates, numbers and quotes, plus any citation you cannot open. The broad statements around them are usually fine — which is exactly what makes the fabricated details easy to miss. Treat specificity as a reason to verify, not a reason to believe.
